title: Talia and the Glittering Glitch
markdown:
The Whispering Range held its stone towers the way a ridge holds barnacles, above ravines that ate light for breakfast and did not give it back at tea. Cloud sat in those gaps as if it paid rent. Talia lived there: mountain-bred, slate-coloured eyes, the sort of elf who trusted a knot more than a shimmer. She noticed the wind’s change before snow, the angle a loose stone preferred when it decided to travel. A well-tied bowline, a sound plank, a plan that stayed a plan — those were her weather. Flash made her shoulders rise toward her ears. Dependable was a warmer word than magic, and she had spent a lifetime preferring it.

Tansy, a snow hare the colour of new fall with a hint of twilight in the fur, usually tumbled downhill like a brook with opinions, ready for a romp the moment a stick looked movable. Soft as moss, if moss had ears that conducted rumours. Today he was planted. Rooted. Heroically still. Those long ears took the wind and did not like what they heard on the far side of the mist.

They stood at a particularly wide and unfriendly ravine, Talia with a length of braided rope that felt honestly itself in her hands, fibre you could trust with a life. “Triple bowline. Across. No wing-spells that fizzle when you need the middle, no teleport that arrives without your feet.” She gave him the practical look she used on loose stones and on people who believed in sparkle. “Engineering. Predictable. Safe, if we do not invent extra weather.”

Tansy did nothing. Nose quivering, dark eyes on something in the mist the far side owned. He might have been a weathered grey rock that had learned stubbornness and decided to teach it.

Talia considered a nudge, a stern word. Then the wind brought a sound too bright for the ravine’s grey: glass bells on a crystal floor, a thousand of them, none of them invited.

A creature of blinding sparkle stepped from the weather, horn catching what little light there was and multiplying it into rude rainbows on the mist. A unicorn. Piffle. Famous not for wisdom but for needing to be looked at, and for glitter that followed him like a rumour he had started. He considered himself the peak of elegance. Talia considered him a delay.

“Oh. You.” She wanted the rope and the proof of it, not an audience.

Piffle tossed a mane that shed iridescent dust onto damp earth. “Talia. Tansy. Magnificent, if a touch earthy. A grand enchantment? The cosmic ballet?” His voice was sugar left too long in the pot.

“We are crossing. Rope. Feet.”

He took this as a cue. “Sensible. Quaint. Terrestrial. Allow sparkle-rific flair.” A flourish of tail; luminous dust meant to make the air itself impressive.

The dust found Talia’s coiled rope and made it a slip. It found Tansy and frosted him into a statue of refusal, specks like a field of fallen stars that had nowhere better to be. He did not become agreeable. He became more Tansy.

“Worse,” Talia said, tight. “Far worse.”

Piffle blinked liquid innocence with a smirk underneath. “Dazzling, surely. Sparkle enhances.”

The whisper of wind became a howl and took his magic with it, a miniature storm of tinkling. Talia felt her own frustration join the weather. Piffle, flustered, doubled down on brilliance. Flustered unicorns, it turned out, made blizzards of a kind. The village’s glow, far across the gap, looked smaller. Cold bit.

She sat on a cold damp rock and felt the chill argue its way inward. Rope slick as a bad intention. Hare immovable. Unicorn still emitting waves of unwelcome shimmer, absorbed in the reflective surface of his own mane. The gap to the village, a distant glow through gathering gloom, yawned wider. The practical crossing she had pictured had dissolved into mist like a poorly tied idea.

Then she noticed what she had been too busy condemning. Tansy, for all his refusal, was warm. The thick frosted fur plus that absolute stillness made a pocket of calm against the rising wind — a tiny furry island in weather that had gotten above itself. Piffle’s scattered dust, annoying as a lecture, caught the weak moonlight and laid small pools of glow across the ravine floor, like gemstones someone had dropped and not bothered to steal. The light was accidental. It was also, inconveniently, useful.

She looked at the problem again, not as an enemy.

“Piffle. Stop being grand. Shine here.” She pointed at the stable lip of rock. “Tansy — stay. You are the point I measure from.”

She did not swing the rope. She tied it to an ancient jut of cliff that had been practising being solid since before festivals. Using the glitter as makeshift lamps and Tansy’s unmoving shape as a survey peg, she gathered stone and fallen branch the wind had not yet claimed, and began a bridge: slow, unflashy, a span made of leftovers and one good knot.

The work took the evening and then some of the night. Ice lived in the wind; grit found her cheeks; the hollow howl tried to unhear itself and failed. Her fingers went numb and then, inconveniently, useful again. Piffle, to his credit, stopped preening and put his beams where she pointed, a whimsical but steady glow that made the next stone visible and the drop honest. Tansy remained a mountain that breathed. A gust stole a branch she had just seated; she lunged, cloak snapping, and put it back with a word the wind did not deserve to keep. Another gust tested the rope’s knot. The knot, being a knot, stayed.

Moon climbed the ink of the sky and laid a silver argument along the unfinished span. From the far glow came muffled laughter — the Winter Hearth Festival, warmth as a rumour, cider as a theory. The sound put another hour in her arms. She laid the last stone as if it were a period. The last branch seated with a thud that satisfied the hands more than any cheer.

She coaxed Tansy. He hopped, stiff, onto the new path. Piffle trotted, glitter toned down to almost modest. The wood creaked and held.

The village smelled of pine and spiced cider. Fires, flushed faces, the square mid-cheer. They stared, then shouted Talia’s name, and Tansy’s, the steady one. Piffle found himself admired for a helpful accident and managed a small bow, horn on a dimmer setting.

Talia’s smile reached her slate eyes. She did not announce that ordinary plans had a magic of their own. She asked for cider, checked the knot once more from this side, and let Tansy sit exactly where he was, which was, for once, the right place.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
